title: Core AI cloud plus three branded subsidiaries
body:
## The Four-Part Architecture

When Nebius Group emerged from the 2024 corporate restructuring that separated Yandex's Russian operating business from the surviving Netherlands holdco, Arkady Volozh inherited not a single asset but a cluster of four distinct businesses, each operating under its own brand, serving different customer bases, and carrying different risk profiles. The largest by revenue and by strategic weight was the core AI cloud — GPU-powered compute infrastructure sold to AI labs, enterprise model developers, and multi-cloud buyers. Around it sat three wholly owned subsidiaries: Toloka AI, a human-data-labelling platform serving the global AI training market; TripleTen, an online tech-education bootcamp targeting data science and software engineering students; and Avride, an autonomous driving research business that sat further from commercial maturity than any of the others. Understanding how those four pieces fit together — and which one was doing the work — was the starting point for any serious analysis of the NBIS equity.

## Core AI Cloud: The Dominant Revenue Engine

The core AI cloud business was, by the time of the Q4 2025 earnings release, the only segment growing fast enough to shape the group's financial trajectory. [Nebius Group Q4 and FY2025 Results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) reported that the core AI cloud segment grew 802% year-over-year in Q4 2025, against a group-level headline of 547% YoY revenue growth to $227.7 million for the quarter. The gap between the segment growth rate and the consolidated rate was, itself, a meaningful piece of information: it indicated that the subsidiary businesses were growing at rates materially below the cloud core, diluting headline growth even as the primary engine accelerated.

The business Nebius was building in that segment was deliberately full-stack. The company procured Nvidia GPU hardware — the H100 and H200 generations that dominated AI training and inference workloads through 2025 — and deployed them inside data centers it designed and operated. The stack did not stop at the hardware layer. Nebius built out the cooling infrastructure, the high-bandwidth networking interconnects, the operating-system-level software, and the developer-facing interfaces that translated physical compute capacity into billable cloud services. Customer access came through two pathways: a self-service platform branded Nebius AI Studio, aimed at AI developers and smaller model-training teams, and direct enterprise contracting for larger, multi-year committed workloads. The enterprise contracting channel was, based on the cash-flow profile, the more consequential one. Q4 operating cash flow of $834 million against Q4 recognised revenue of $227.7 million was the signature of a business collecting prepayments from enterprise customers well in advance of revenue recognition — a pattern consistent with hyperscaler-adjacent multi-year compute contracts rather than spot-market GPU rental.

The geographic footprint at the close of FY2025 was predominantly European. Legacy data center infrastructure in Finland, inherited from the Yandex-era build-out, formed the earliest operational base. US expansion was underway through 2025 and into 2026, though specific US site locations were not separately disclosed in the public filings at the snapshot date. The contracted-power picture told the more precise capacity story: 170 megawatts of active power at year-end 2025, against more than 2,000 megawatts contracted — a ratio of roughly 12-to-1 between pipeline and deployed capacity, representing either an extraordinary forward-commitment book or, depending on execution confidence, the single largest operational risk on the balance sheet.

The Nvidia relationship was the structural variable that distinguished Nebius from most of its peer group. In August 2025, Nebius completed a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement with Accel, Nvidia, and certain accounts of Orbis Investments. [Nebius $700M Strategic Equity Financing](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-announces-oversubscribed-strategic-equity-financing-of-usd-700-million-to-accelerate-roll-out-of-full-stack-ai-infrastructure) Nvidia's participation was dual-role: it was simultaneously the company's primary GPU supplier and a minority equity investor with an aligned financial interest in Nebius's capacity expansion. The implied consequence — that Nebius would receive preferential allocation treatment within Nvidia's constrained GPU output pipeline relative to buyers without equity alignment — was not disclosed as an explicit contractual term but was broadly understood by the investor community as one of the practical benefits of the structure. Specific GPU allocation volumes were not publicly disclosed.

## Toloka AI: The Data-Labelling Complement

Toloka AI operated a crowd-sourced human-data-labelling platform serving AI model developers who needed ground-truth annotation for vision, language, and multimodal training datasets. The business pre-dated the Nebius restructuring, having operated within the Yandex ecosystem as a platform for distributed human intelligence tasks. Under Nebius Group ownership, Toloka was positioned as a complementary revenue line to the core cloud: customers building or fine-tuning AI models frequently needed both compute (which Nebius's cloud provided) and annotated training data (which Toloka supplied). The customer overlap between the two businesses was the strategic logic for keeping them under a single corporate roof rather than spinning Toloka into a standalone entity.

The revenue model was service-based, with hyperscaler-adjacent AI labs and enterprise AI teams among the disclosed customer categories. Toloka competed in a market that included Scale AI, Surge AI, and proprietary internal annotation operations run by the major AI labs themselves. Separate revenue figures for Toloka were not disclosed in the publicly available segment reporting at the snapshot date — the filing basis was consolidated, with the core AI cloud Q4 YoY growth rate of +802% as the cleanest publicly available breakdown.

## TripleTen: The Education Vertical

TripleTen was the most conventionally consumer-facing of the three subsidiaries. The business offered online bootcamp-style courses in data science, software engineering, and AI/ML skills, targeting adult learners seeking career transitions or upskilling in technology disciplines. It operated with its own management team and brand identity, sitting within the Nebius Group consolidated perimeter but functionally independent.

The strategic rationale for retaining TripleTen within the group was less obvious than for Toloka. Tech education was a market with its own competitive dynamics — dominated by platforms such as Coursera, Udemy, and direct university extension programs — and the revenue profile was unlikely to scale proportionally to the AI cloud core. Group management had not publicly indicated plans to separate TripleTen as of the snapshot date, and the business continued to consolidate into group financials without separate revenue disclosure.

## Avride: The Long-Cycle Moonshot

Avride was the business furthest from near-term commercial relevance but carrying the longest potential upside horizon. The autonomous driving and robotics platform was characterised in the group's investor communications as a long-cycle R&D holding — the closest peer analogies were Waymo (Alphabet subsidiary), Aurora Innovation, or the earlier-stage development phase of Cruise (General Motors). Like those peers, Avride consumed capital in pursuit of technical milestones that would precede any commercial deployment at scale. It contributed no material revenue to the FY2025 consolidated results.

The group's retention of Avride reflected, in part, the talent and intellectual-property base that had survived the restructuring from Yandex. Yandex had operated a self-driving research program, SDG, that was among the more sophisticated autonomous-vehicle efforts outside the United States and China during its active phase. What Avride inherited of that program's personnel and technology remained a disclosed but detail-sparse element of the group's asset base. Avride's path to monetisation — licensing, strategic partnership, or independent market entry — was unresolved within the snapshot window.

## Revenue Mix and Disclosure Constraints

The segment architecture was clear at the product-brand level. The revenue arithmetic within it was not. Nebius did not separately disclose product-line revenue for Toloka, TripleTen, or Avride in the publicly summarised FY2025 filings or the Q4 earnings release. The disclosable figure that most closely captured the core AI cloud contribution was the +802% Q4 YoY growth rate — a rate that implied the core segment's absolute revenue substantially dominated the consolidated $227.7 million Q4 print, with the three subsidiaries contributing the residual. Analysts and investors modelling the business were working from that implied split rather than stated segment financials.

| Metric | Q4 2025 | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Group revenue | $227.7M | $3.0–3.4B |
| Core AI cloud YoY growth | +802% | Not separately guided |
| Annualised run rate (ARR) | $1.25B exit-2025 | $7–9B |
| ARR contracted share | — | >50% |
| Active power | 170MW | 800–1,000MW |
| Capex | ~$2B (Q4 only) | $16–20B |

[Source: Nebius Group Q4 and FY2025 Results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results)

## Structural Position: The Advantages and the Asymmetric Risk

The balance-sheet endowment that Nebius carried into FY2026 was genuinely unusual in its competitive set. $3.7 billion of cash at year-end 2025, augmented by the $834 million Q4 operating cash flow, gave the group a funding runway for the $16–20 billion FY2026 capex programme that no pure-play AI cloud competitor without direct balance-sheet backing could replicate unassisted. CoreWeave, the most comparable public peer, had accessed debt markets at scale to fund its build; Nebius entered FY2026 with equity capital already in place and contracted ARR covering more than half of the $7–9 billion target.

The structural disadvantage was the starting position. Nebius was ramping from a post-restructuring base, not from a multi-year operating history as an independent AI cloud company. The 170 megawatts of active power against 2,000-plus megawatts contracted was a gap that required simultaneous execution across power utility agreements, real estate site development, Nvidia GPU delivery schedules, mechanical and electrical construction, and customer onboarding — in multiple geographies, in a single fiscal year. That execution complexity, rather than any question of demand or funding, was the primary risk the group's FY2026 guidance embedded.
